summary: DELTAHEAT is a web tool that answers one question for any city, district or hand-drawn area in Ukraine: is this place heating up faster than the nature around it, and is that change real? Using NASA/USGS Landsat 8 land surface temperature for every summer from 2013 to 2025, it compares built-up land with the nearby stable forest that lives under the same weather, so hot and cool summers cancel out. It then reports the four things the challenge asks for: what is changing (surface heat), where (any place, on a 60 m grid), how much (degrees per decade, Theil-Sen slope) and whether the trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall test). If the change is not significant, the tool says so plainly. In Kyiv it shows opposite significant trends a few kilometres apart: the gap grows by 1.9 °C per decade in one neighbourhood and shrinks by 2.5 °C per decade in another, while the city as a whole shows no significant change. Residents, students, city planners and scientists get one sentence, one number and one chart, with map layers, a built-in AI chat and data export behind them.
details:
What the Project Does


DELTAHEAT answers one focused question: "Is my neighborhood or city getting hotter than the surrounding nature — and is that a statistically significant change rather than random weather variation?" It was built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

How It Works


1. Selecting an Area and Time Period: Users can choose a preset city or district, search any Ukrainian address via OpenStreetMap Nominatim, or draw a custom circle or polygon on the map, and select the analysis years (2013–2025 by default, or any custom window of at least 8 valid years for significance testing).
2. Comparing Against a Natural Forest Baseline: Raw summer Land Surface Temperature (LST) fluctuates from year to year with regional weather. To isolate the urban signal, DELTAHEAT defines a stable natural forest baseline in a 2–15 km ring outside the city boundary (excluding farmland and water) as a shared reference for the city, and computes the summer temperature gap (in degrees Celsius) between built-up land and that forest.
3. Tracking Land-Cover Changes Over Time: Using annual land-cover maps (Esri LULC 2017–2023 extended to 2013–2016 and 2024–2025 via Landsat 8 NDVI and NDBI thresholds) on an aligned 60 m EPSG:3035 grid, pixels are separated into: (a) always-built pixels (used for the headline trend so shifts in land composition do not create artificial temperature trends), (b) newly built-up pixels (showing the temperature gap before vs. after construction), and (c) urban parks and green areas inside the city.
4. Per-Scene Calculation to Remove Orbital Swath Seams: Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Lviv span overlapping Landsat 8 WRS-2 paths where differing overpass dates create artificial temperature jumps across swath borders in simple seasonal composites. For these cities, DELTAHEAT computes the heat gap within each individual clear-sky acquisition date before taking the summer median, reducing inter-annual noise (for example, in Pozniaky, standard deviation drops from 2.29 °C to 0.93 °C). Across the rest of Ukraine, summer composites and an automatically derived forest ring are used.
5. Statistical Significance and Honest Verdicts: Trend slopes are estimated with the non-parametric Theil-Sen estimator (°C per decade with 95% confidence intervals) and tested for significance with the two-sided Mann-Kendall test (significant when p < 0.05 with at least 8 valid years). When p >= 0.05, DELTAHEAT explicitly reports "not significant yet" and explains physical reasons (inter-annual weather variability, morning building shadows around the ~10:45–11:00 local overpass, or gradual tree canopy growth).

Real Data Examples in Kyiv (2013–2025)


1. Nyzhni Sady, Osokorky (densifying former dacha area): Mean gap +5.1 °C, trend +1.88 °C per decade (rounded +1.9 °C per decade), Mann-Kendall p = 0.002 (Significant). The thermal gap with the forest is growing alongside a 25% increase in sealed surface in GHSL.
2. Desnianske cottage town, Troieshchyna (maturing gardens): Mean gap +8.5 °C, trend -2.53 °C per decade (rounded -2.5 °C per decade), Mann-Kendall p = 0.033 (Significant). The thermal gap is shrinking as trees and gardens matured (NDVI trend +0.109 per decade, p = 0.003).
3. Pozniaky (~1 km dense residential area): Mean gap +11.4 °C, trend +0.40 °C per decade, p = 0.37 (Not significant). Persistently hot across all 13 summers without a statistically significant change in the gap.
4. Kyiv as a whole: Mean gap +7.98 °C (rounded +8.0 °C), trend +0.48 °C per decade, p = 0.76 (Not significant).
5. Holosiivskyi Forest (control zone inside the city): Mean gap -0.15 °C, trend +0.32 °C per decade, p = 0.50 (Not significant) — behaves like the surrounding forest baseline.

Interface Features and Technology Stack


Interactive Web Interface: MapLibre GL map switching between Heat Gap vs. Forest, Land Surface Temperature, Greenness (NDVI), Greenness Change since 2013, and satellite imagery; hotspot pins inside analyzed zones; Detailed Analysis view with yearly charts, excluded-year explanations, CMIP6 air-temperature reference projections, report export (PDF, XLSX, CSV, JSON), and explicit map overlays for USGS ASTER GED emissivity gaps, low-scene swaths, and temporarily occupied territories.
Backend and Geospatial Engine: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, GDAL, Shapely, PyProj, ReportLab, OpenPyXL, Pytest.
Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Fontsource (Onest), custom SVG charts, Playwright, Vitest.
Optional Analyst Panel: Anthropic Claude Python SDK reads precomputed backend numbers via read-only tools (zero math inside the language model) to answer user questions; a deterministic backend validator checks every cited number, and the core application works standalone without requiring the language model.
